terms.definition: A software-based computer created by a hypervisor on a physical server. Each VM has its own full operating system and pre-allocated CPU, RAM, and disk resources.
terms.example: An EC2 instance in AWS is a virtual machine. You can run multiple EC2 instances on the same physical AWS data center hardware.

terms.definition: Software that creates and manages virtual machines by partitioning physical server resources. Sits between hardware and VMs.
terms.example: VMware, Oracle VirtualBox, Xen, and KVM are popular hypervisors. AWS uses Xen and Nitro hypervisors for EC2.

terms.definition: A lightweight, isolated process that packages an application with its libraries and dependencies, sharing the host OS kernel instead of running a full OS.
terms.example: A Node.js web server packaged in a container includes only Node.js, the app code, and npm packages — not a full OS.

terms.definition: The process of packaging applications into containers to achieve environment consistency, isolation, and portability across different systems.
terms.example: Packaging a Python Flask app into a Docker container so it runs identically on a developer laptop and in an AWS EC2 instance.

terms.definition: The most popular containerization platform. Provides tools to build Docker images, run containers, and push images to registries.
terms.example: You install Docker on your EC2, write a Dockerfile, run docker build to create an image, and docker run to start a container.

terms.definition: A plain text file with step-by-step instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD) that Docker reads to build a container image. Acts as a blueprint for the container.
terms.example: A Dockerfile for a Python app starts with FROM python:3.11, then copies the app files, runs pip install, and sets CMD to start the app.

terms.definition: A read-only, layered template built from a Dockerfile. Contains everything needed to run an application: base OS, runtime, libraries, and app code.
terms.example: The nginx:latest image on Docker Hub contains a minimal Linux base, the Nginx web server, and all required config files.

terms.definition: A running instance of a Docker image. A live, isolated process executing the application in its own filesystem and network namespace.
terms.example: Running docker run -d -p 80:80 nginx creates a container from the nginx image, running Nginx and serving web traffic on port 80.

terms.definition: The background service (dockerd) that actually builds images, manages containers, and handles all Docker operations. Receives instructions from the Docker Client.
terms.example: When you type docker build, the Docker CLI sends that request to the daemon running in the background, which does the actual build work.

terms.definition: The most popular public Docker image registry where developers push custom images and pull official base images like nginx, python, and ubuntu.
terms.example: Running docker pull python:3.11 downloads the official Python 3.11 image from Docker Hub to your local machine.

terms.definition: Amazon Elastic Container Registry — AWS's managed Docker image registry. Stores Docker images privately and integrates with ECS and EKS.
terms.example: After building a Docker image in CI, you push it to ECR using docker push. ECS then pulls it from ECR when deploying.

terms.definition: An automated workflow that builds, tests, and deploys code every time a developer makes a change. CI handles build and test; CD handles deployment.
terms.example: A Jenkins pipeline that triggers on every git push, runs Maven build, SonarQube analysis, JUnit tests, and deploys to dev automatically.

terms.definition: The practice of automatically building and testing code on every push or pull request, catching bugs early and preventing broken code from entering the main branch.
terms.example: Every time a developer pushes to their feature branch, Jenkins automatically compiles the code and runs unit tests within minutes.

terms.definition: The practice of keeping code always ready to deploy to production. A human manually approves the final deployment to production.
terms.example: The CD pipeline deploys automatically to dev and QA. Production deployment requires a manager to click an approval button.

terms.definition: Analyzing source code without running it to find bugs, security vulnerabilities, code smells, and poor coding practices. SonarQube is the most popular tool.
terms.example: SonarQube scans a Java file and flags a hardcoded database password as a critical security vulnerability without ever running the app.

terms.definition: Automated tests that verify small, individual units of code (functions or methods) work correctly in isolation. JUnit for Java, PyTest for Python.
terms.example: A JUnit test checks that the calculateTax() function returns 18.0 when passed 100.0 as input.

terms.definition: A distributed version control system installed locally. Tracks all versions of files in a .git repository folder. Used with git add, git commit, and git push.
terms.example: After editing app.py, you run git add app.py, then git commit -m 'fix login bug' to save a new version in the local .git folder.

terms.definition: A formal request in GitHub or GitLab to merge a feature branch into the main branch. Triggers CI checks and requires human code review before approval.
terms.example: After finishing the login feature, a developer raises a PR on GitHub. Jenkins runs tests automatically. The team lead reviews and approves the merge.

terms.definition: A separate Git branch created for developing a specific feature. Keeps work isolated from the main branch until it is reviewed and approved.
terms.example: A developer creates branch feature/payment-gateway to build the payment service. Only after CI passes and PR approval does it merge to main.

terms.definition: An open-source container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, self-healing, and load balancing of containerized applications across a cluster.
terms.example: Kubernetes detects that a payment service pod has crashed and automatically restarts it on a healthy node within seconds.

terms.definition: An architectural style where an application is built as small, independent services — each with its own codebase, database, and container — that communicate via APIs.
terms.example: An e-commerce app with separate Login, Cart, Payment, and Delivery services, each running in its own Docker container on Kubernetes.

terms.definition: The practice of managing and provisioning cloud infrastructure using code and configuration files instead of manual clicks. Terraform and Ansible are common tools.
terms.example: A Terraform file defines an EC2 t3.medium instance. Running terraform apply creates that exact instance in AWS automatically.

terms.definition: An automatic HTTP notification sent by GitHub to a CI tool (like Jenkins) whenever a code push or PR event occurs, triggering the pipeline.
terms.example: When a developer pushes to main on GitHub, GitHub sends a webhook to Jenkins, which immediately starts the CI build pipeline.

terms.definition: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service — AWS's fully managed Kubernetes service. AWS manages the control plane; you deploy your workloads on the worker nodes.
terms.example: Instead of manually setting up a Kubernetes cluster, you create an EKS cluster and deploy your microservices as Kubernetes Deployments and Services.
